El principio de mínimo privilegio, ya co: The principle of least privilege, already well known in traditional identity security, takes on a different urgency when applied to AI agents, because an agent can be manipulated into misusing any permission it has available, even if the user never requested that action. Applying it in practice means an agent designed to summarize documents shouldn't have credentials with write permission on the file system, and a financial analysis skill doesn't need access to the user's emails just because they share the same agent session. The particular challenge with agents is that their capabilities are usually configured in aggregate, connecting several tools to the same assistant for convenience, which easily ends up implicitly granting permissions no individual task justifies. An effective practice is to define specific permission profiles per task or per activated skill, revoking access to tools not used in that particular session, and periodically reviewing which agents accumulate broad privileges "just in case", since that silent accumulation is exactly what an attacker looks to exploit when compromising an agent through instruction manipulation.
Auditar cada acción tomada por un agente: Auditing every action taken by an autonomous agent
Cuando un agente actúa de forma autónoma: When an agent acts autonomously, the question a security team needs to be able to answer after an incident isn't just what the model said, but exactly which actions it carried out, with what parameters, on which resources and in response to what input, and without a detailed log of each step that reconstruction becomes impossible. An effective log for agents captures the complete chain of reasoning and action: the original instruction received, the tools invoked along with the exact arguments used, the response obtained from each one, and the final decision made, not just a high-level summary of the result. This traceability is especially important for detecting successful prompt injection attacks after the fact, because it makes it possible to identify the exact point where the agent's behavior deviated from what was expected after processing a specific external data source. Besides serving forensic investigation, these logs feed real-time monitoring systems that can alert on anomalous patterns, such as an agent that suddenly invokes a tool it never uses in its normal flow, making it possible to intervene before the action is completed.
Aislar la ejecución del agente para cont: Isolating the agent's execution to contain errors
El sandboxing consiste en ejecutar las a: Sandboxing consists of running an agent's actions inside an isolated, controlled environment, so that if the agent makes a mistake or is manipulated into acting maliciously, the damage stays contained within that environment and doesn't spread to critical production systems. This is especially relevant when the agent runs dynamically generated code, something increasingly common in programming assistants, where allowing direct execution on the developer's machine or on a production server without any isolation is equivalent to giving an untrusted process full access to the system. A well-designed sandbox limits not only the accessible file system and network, but also execution time and available compute resources, preventing an infinite loop or a deliberate attempt to exhaust resources from affecting other services. Beyond technical isolation, limiting the scope of actions means explicitly defining a list of permitted operations per context, so an agent used for data analysis doesn't, by default, have the ability to delete files or modify system settings, even if it technically could.

Checklist de riesgo previo al despliegue: Risk checklist before deploying an agent
Antes de poner en producción cualquier s: Before putting any agent-based solution into production, it's worth applying a structured risk assessment that goes beyond validating that the functionality meets the intended use case, because an agent that works correctly under normal conditions can represent a severe risk under adversarial manipulation that was never tested. This assessment must answer concrete questions: which tools the agent has connected and what an attacker could do with each one if they manage to control its instructions, which sensitive data it may touch during normal operation, which actions are reversible and which aren't, and what human approval mechanisms or automatic limits exist to contain unexpected behavior. A useful practical criterion is to classify risk according to the product of the potential impact of an action and the likelihood that existing defenses fail to stop it, prioritizing additional controls where both factors are high, for example an agent with access to financial transactions and no human confirmation step. Skipping this assessment under launch time pressure is, in practice, the most common cause of security incidents in early deployments of autonomous agents.

Un agente en producción no se comporta c: An agent in production doesn't behave like a static system; its responses and actions vary according to the context of each conversation, which makes defining what's "normal" more complex than in a traditional system based on fixed rules, and that's precisely why continuous monitoring is essential, not optional. Establishing a baseline of expected behavior per task type makes it possible to detect significant deviations, such as a support agent that suddenly starts invoking administrative tools outside its usual pattern, or a skill that generates an unusual volume of calls to an external API in a short period, signals that usually indicate successful manipulation or a serious configuration error. The response to these anomalies should be automated at least in its first phase, with the ability to temporarily suspend the agent's permissions or pause the active session while a human investigates, instead of relying exclusively on later manual review that comes too late to prevent the damage. One element that distinguishes a mature program is feeding these incidents back into the agent's design, adjusting permissions, input filters or human approval rules according to the abuse patterns actually observed in production.
Cuándo exigir aprobación humana antes de: When to require human approval before acting
Human in the loop es el diseño donde un: Human in the loop is the design in which an agent, before carrying out a high-impact action, stops and requests explicit confirmation from a person instead of proceeding fully autonomously, and it's one of the most effective controls available today to contain the risk of the model's erroneous or manipulated decisions. The key is deciding judiciously which actions require that pause and which don't, because requiring approval for every trivial step eliminates the practical value of automating with agents, while not requiring it for irreversible actions, such as money transfers, data deletion or sending external communications, leaves the door open to costly mistakes with no possibility of correction. A mature approach classifies actions by risk level and irreversibility, letting the agent autonomously carry out low-impact, reversible tasks, such as generating a draft or querying information, while reserving human approval for what really justifies it. An important nuance is that the approval must show the person enough context to decide judiciously, not just a generic confirm button, because an approval given without really understanding what's being authorized provides no real protection.

Cómo los cambios de negocio amplían el r: How business changes expand cyber risk
Cada movimiento estructural de una organ: Every structural move an organization makes, whether opening a new market, bringing on a technology vendor or an internal reorganization, changes the attack surface available to an adversary. New systems, integrations and users connect to the environment before security controls finish adapting, and that time lag is precisely what attackers look to exploit. Understanding this relationship matters because it makes it possible to anticipate risk instead of reacting after an incident, involving security from the design of the change and not as a final formality. A common example is migrating a business area to a new SaaS platform, where temporary emergency access is enabled that's rarely revoked in time, leaving orphaned accounts with excessive privileges months after the project is completed.
El papel de seguridad como socio del cam: Security's role as a partner in change
Cuando ciberseguridad se involucra única: When cybersecurity only gets involved at the end of a change project, its role is reduced to signing off on a risk already taken on; when it participates from the start, it can influence architecture, contract and schedule decisions before they become costly to fix. The security team should act as a technical advisor within change committees, translating risk findings into terms the business understands, instead of blocking initiatives without offering viable alternatives. This requires a constant presence in change governance forums, not just one-off assessments. In practice, a well-integrated role shows when security proposes a phased migration path with compensating controls, instead of simply objecting to an aggressive deadline set by leadership to launch a new product.
Panorama de cambios que impactan la segu: Overview of changes that impact security
No todos los cambios organizacionales ex: Not all organizational changes expose the same type of risk, and distinguishing them is the first step in prioritizing security efforts. A merger usually involves connecting two networks with different maturity levels, an acquisition adds legacy assets and applications whose real patch status is unknown until audited, and an internal restructuring redistributes access and responsibilities in a way that can leave privileges without a clear owner. Classifying the type of change makes it possible to apply a specific risk checklist instead of a generic approach that ignores the particularities of each scenario. For example, in a small startup acquisition, the main risk is almost always shared credentials and unreviewed source code, while in a restructuring the focus should be on the timely revocation of access for relocated staff.
La debida diligencia de ciberseguridad b: Cybersecurity due diligence seeks to answer a concrete question before closing an M&A deal: whether the target company hides security liabilities that could translate into economic or legal losses after the purchase. This includes reviewing its incident history, regulatory compliance, network architecture, third-party contracts and the maturity of its vulnerability management practices, ideally with limited but direct access to technical evidence and not just questionnaires answered by the seller. Its practical importance lies in the fact that a serious finding can adjust the transaction price, make closing conditional on prior remediation or even cancel the deal. A recurring case is discovering, well into the process, that the target company suffered an undisclosed data breach, which forces renegotiating terms and planning regulatory notifications before integrating systems.
Diagnóstico técnico de seguridad del adq: Technical security diagnosis of the acquired company
Más allá de la revisión documental inici: Beyond the initial document review, assessing the security posture of the acquired entity involves a concrete technical diagnosis: an asset inventory, analysis of exposed vulnerabilities, review of cloud configurations, and verification of access and identity controls. This work is usually done in two stages, one before closing with information limited by confidentiality agreements, and another after closing with full access, when it's possible to run internal scans and interview the local technical team. Its practical value lies in building a prioritized risk map that avoids treating an outdated version of an internal server the same as a publicly exposed customer database. A typical example is finding an internet-accessible administration panel without multi-factor authentication, something that rarely appears in the documentation provided by the seller but that an external scan detects in minutes.

Conectar redes de forma segura tras una: Connecting networks securely after an M&A
Una vez cerrada la operación, conectar l: Once the deal is closed, connecting two organizations' infrastructure is one of the riskiest moments of the whole process, because networks with different levels of segmentation, different identity providers and different patching policies are combined under business time pressure to show synergies quickly. Secure integration prioritizes first establishing a controlled bridge, with segmentation and reinforced monitoring, instead of merging directories or opening network routes en masse from day one. This reduces the chance that an undetected weakness in the acquired entity spreads to the main network. In practice, many teams choose to keep both environments isolated for months, connected only through a small set of validated services, while security controls are harmonized and critical systems are migrated as planned.
Trazabilidad y aprobación formal de camb: Traceability and formal approval of changes
El control de versiones y la aprobación: Version control and formal approval of critical changes are the mechanisms that prevent a code or configuration change from reaching production without having been reviewed by someone other than its author. A well-used version control system records who changed what, when and why, while an approval process requires high-impact changes, such as changes to firewall rules, database permissions or infrastructure deployments, to go through a security owner before being carried out. This matters because most serious production incidents don't come from sophisticated attacks but from poorly validated changes applied at the wrong moment. A concrete example is requiring double approval and a scheduled maintenance window for any change to cloud access rules, preventing an urgent Friday-afternoon change from opening a port nobody ever closes again.
Adoptar una nueva tecnología, ya sea una: Adopting a new technology, whether an artificial intelligence tool, an additional cloud provider or a low-code platform, brings business benefits but also risks that are rarely visible until the tool is already in widespread use. Assessing that risk early means reviewing where data is stored, which certifications the vendor holds, how access is managed and what dependencies the organization creates on a third party. This analysis should be done before signing contracts or before a business area adopts the tool on its own, because reversing an already widespread adoption is much costlier than stopping it in time. A frequent case is employees' unauthorized use of artificial intelligence assistants, who end up sharing sensitive company information with an external service without a data processing agreement in place.
Gestionar el cambio en la infraestructur: Managing change in technology infrastructure securely means applying a consistent framework (impact assessment, maintenance window, rollback plan and subsequent validation) to every relevant change to servers, networks or cloud services, regardless of the urgency perceived by whoever requests it. The discipline here lies in resisting the temptation to skip steps when business pressure is high, because that's precisely when the likelihood of introducing a vulnerability or a service outage increases. Having a tested rollback plan, and not just a documented one, is what really reduces recovery time when something goes wrong. An illustrative example is updating an identity management system, where skipping the rollback plan can leave the whole organization without access for hours if the new configuration fails in production.

Traducir el riesgo técnico a decisiones: Translating technical risk into business decisions
Comunicar el riesgo cibernético a quiene: Communicating cyber risk to those leading a change process requires translating technical findings into terms that affect business decisions (deadlines, costs, reputation), instead of reporting vulnerabilities on severity scales that only make sense to another security engineer. A transformation leader needs to know what concrete risk they take on by keeping an aggressive schedule, and what alternatives exist to mitigate it without stopping the project entirely. This matters because the lack of this translation is the most common reason security is left out of important decisions, not out of ill will but because the message never arrived in an actionable format. An effective example is presenting the risk as an estimated range of financial impact and an exposure period, instead of a list of technical findings with no associated business context.
Control de accesos ante cambios de perso: Access control in the face of staff changes
Durante una reestructuración, el volumen: During a restructuring, the volume of role changes, transfers between areas and staff departures grows far above the usual pace, and with it the likelihood of access being granted that no longer matches a person's real function. Managing this securely requires an agile privilege review process, ideally automated, that revokes access at the moment of the role change and not weeks later when someone notices the inconsistency in an audit. The practical importance is direct: accounts with privileges accumulated from previous roles are one of the most exploited vectors in insider incidents, whether through human error or deliberate misuse. A common example is an employee who moves from a technical area to a sales area and keeps administrative access to critical systems they no longer need for their new position for months.

Sostener controles clave mientras dura e: Sustaining key controls throughout the change
Durante una transformación organizaciona: During an organizational transformation, existing security controls risk being put on hold while the team's attention is focused on the change project, leaving monitoring gaps or unapplied patches precisely when the environment is most unstable and most attractive to an attacker. Keeping these controls active means explicitly defining which security processes can't be interrupted under any circumstances (patch management, event monitoring and incident response) and assigning clear owners to sustain them even if the rest of the team is focused on the transition. This matters because attackers know the pattern of organizations lowering their guard during big changes well. A practical example is assigning a person dedicated exclusively to reviewing security alerts throughout a migration, while the rest of the team carries out the technical project.
Mantener las políticas alineadas con el: Keeping policies aligned with the business
Las políticas de seguridad que funcionab: Security policies that worked for an organization of a certain size or business model usually become obsolete when the company changes scale, enters new markets or adopts new operating models, and an outdated policy creates two equally damaging problems: controls that no longer cover real risks, and rules the business ignores because it considers them irrelevant. Updating policies periodically, and not only after an incident, keeps them a credible reference for the organization. This requires a formal review process tied to relevant business milestones, not just a fixed annual calendar that may come too late. A clear example is a data classification policy written for a local business, which stops being enough as soon as the company starts operating under other countries' data protection regulations after an international expansion.
Un comité de gestión del cambio seguro e: A secure change management committee is the formal space where change initiatives with relevant security implications are reviewed and approved, bringing together representatives from technology, security, legal and the business to assess risk jointly before authorizing execution. Its practical value lies in preventing risk decisions from being concentrated in a single person or area, and in leaving an auditable record of why each significant change was approved or rejected. For it to really work, the committee needs clear criteria for which changes require its review, avoiding both excessive bureaucracy over minor changes and the omission of critical changes for lack of a defined threshold. A typical example of how it works is requiring the committee's sign-off before migrating a payroll system to a new external provider, given the volume of sensitive data involved.

Cada proceso de cambio deja evidencia co: Every change process leaves concrete evidence of what worked and what failed in terms of security, but that information only has value if it's collected systematically and turned into real adjustments to future processes, instead of remaining in the informal memory of those who took part. Documenting lessons learned after a merger, a technology migration or a restructuring makes it possible to identify recurring patterns, such as which types of access tend to go unrevoked or which controls get skipped under time pressure, and to fix them before the next similar project. This matters because organizations that don't close this loop tend to repeat the same security mistakes with each change, even when the people involved change. Cómo distinguir BCP, DRP y gestión de cr: How to distinguish BCP, DRP and crisis management
Es común confundir estos tres conceptos: It's common to confuse these three concepts because they're usually activated together in response to the same event, but each answers a different question and requires its own documents and owners. The BCP, or business continuity plan, defines how the organization keeps its critical processes running for the duration of a disruption, regardless of the cause. The DRP, or disaster recovery plan, focuses specifically on restoring the technology infrastructure that supports those processes: servers, networks, systems. Crisis management, on the other hand, coordinates decision-making at the highest level, external communication and reputation during the event, without going into the operational detail of the other two. Understanding this separation matters because activating the wrong plan delays the response; for example, treating a high-profile cyberattack only as a technical DRP problem without activating crisis management can leave the organization without a coordinated message to customers and the media.

Un plan de continuidad sin roles clarame: A continuity plan without clearly assigned roles becomes a theoretical document nobody knows how to carry out when the real disruption happens. This matters in practice because in a crisis there's no time to improvise hierarchies or wait for someone to take the lead on their own initiative. A frequent mistake is assigning responsibility to a single person with no backup, so if that person is on vacation or is precisely the one affected by the incident, as happens when the IT lead is also the victim of a targeted phishing attack, the plan is left with nobody to activate it.

These two values must be defined per critical process and not generically for the whole organization, because a billing system may tolerate hours of disruption while an online payments platform may need an RTO of minutes. Their practical importance lies in the fact that they directly determine how much the organization must invest in redundancy, data replication and backup capacity: investing too much is waste and too little is risk taken on without a conscious decision. A key nuance is that an ambitious RPO, close to zero, usually requires real-time replication, which is much costlier than a traditional daily backup.

This identification is done by interviewing the owners of each business process, not just the technology area, because those who best know the real impact of an outage are the ones who run the process day to day. From there, differentiated recovery times are assigned, avoiding the common mistake of treating all systems as equally urgent, which in practice ends up meaning none is recovered in time for lack of clear prioritization. A typical example is discovering that a system technology considered secondary turns out to be critical for meeting a daily regulatory obligation, and so must move up the recovery priority list.

The choice depends directly on the recovery times defined in the BIA and on the available budget, because a hot site is significantly costlier to maintain. A practical example in modern environments is using a cloud provider's secondary region as an alternate site, automatically replicating critical data without maintaining duplicate physical hardware.

This matters because every minute lost deciding whether or not to activate the plan is recovery time irreversibly lost. There's no single right strategy for every process, and the most common mistake is applying the same costly solution to processes with different levels of criticality or, worse, having no defined strategy for processes that do need one. Weighing the cost of each option against the cost of the disruption is what makes it possible to reach a reasonable decision instead of one based on intuition. A practical example is keeping a documented manual procedure for processing orders on paper during a sales system outage, while the digital platform is restored.

During onboarding, the risk lies in granting excessive access from the start, beyond what the role really requires. During employment, the risk appears when access isn't adjusted as the person changes role or project, accumulating unnecessary privileges over time. And at departure, the most critical risk is failing to revoke all access in time, leaving active accounts nobody should be able to use anymore. Seeing security as a continuous process tied to each stage of this cycle, and not as an isolated review, prevents access gaps from silently accumulating over time.

A hiring process without proper verification can bring someone with malicious intentions into a sensitive role, while a slow offboarding process can leave a disgruntled former employee's account active. Recognizing this relationship lets HR stop seeing security as a purely technical issue and start incorporating simple controls, such as timely coordination with IT, into its own usual people management processes.

HR usually handles background checks, signing confidentiality agreements and timely notification of staff hires, changes and departures. Security, for its part, translates that information into concrete technical actions: granting, adjusting or revoking access to systems as appropriate. The most common point of failure is precisely at the boundary between the two areas, when HR handles a departure but doesn't communicate it to security in time, or vice versa. Defining in writing who notifies what, to whom and within what time frame prevents these communication gaps from turning into improper access with nobody responsible for closing it.

It's not enough to have them signed as an administrative formality: explaining their content during onboarding, with concrete examples of which behaviors would violate the agreement, considerably increases their practical effectiveness compared with simply handing them over as one more document among dozens of hiring papers.

Qué es un marco de gestión de riesgo de: What a third-party risk management framework is
Un marco de Third Party Risk Management: A Third Party Risk Management framework systematically structures the entire lifecycle of the relationship with a vendor from a risk perspective, starting with due diligence before contracting, through the formal assessment, the negotiation of contractual clauses and monitoring during the relationship, and ending with a secure offboarding process that revokes access and verifies the destruction of shared data. Adopting a recognized framework, instead of isolated processes created by different areas without coordination, lets purchasing, legal, security and the business areas speak the same language about third-party risk and avoid duplicating efforts or leaving gaps between stages. The absence of a formal framework usually means each area manages vendor risk its own way: purchasing evaluates price, legal reviews the contract and security learns about the relationship once it's already signed, with no real time to influence the agreed terms.
Visión general del riesgo en la cadena d: A general view of supply chain risk
La cadena de suministro se ha convertido: The supply chain has become one of the most exploited attack vectors, because compromising a vendor with weaker security controls is usually easier than directly attacking the target organization, and that vendor often already has legitimate access to internal systems or data. This risk ranges from software vendors that distribute compromised updates to service providers that handle sensitive data or maintain direct connections to the internal network. The picture gets more complicated because the risk doesn't end with the direct vendor but extends to that vendor's subcontractors, forming a chain of dependencies many organizations haven't even mapped. Understanding this landscape realistically, instead of assuming security ends at your own perimeter, is the starting point for justifying investment in a formal third-party risk management program.
Cómo varía el riesgo según el tipo de te: How risk varies by type of third party
El término tercero abarca una variedad a: The term third party covers a wide variety of relationships with very different risk profiles: software vendors that process data directly, cloud infrastructure providers that host critical systems, consultants with temporary access to sensitive information, and general service providers with no connection to the organization's systems. Each type exposes the organization differently: a software vendor with access to the codebase can introduce vulnerabilities directly into the product, while a logistics provider with access only to shipping data represents a much more limited exposure risk. Understanding this variety makes it possible to design differentiated assessment processes instead of a single generic form, and avoids the common mistake of underestimating vendors that, although they seem low-profile because of the type of service they provide, end up having a level of technical access disproportionate to their apparent business relevance.
Cómo clasificar proveedores por nivel de: How to classify vendors by risk level
No todos los proveedores representan el: Not all vendors represent the same level of risk, and applying the same assessment process to all of them consumes resources inefficiently while leaving those that can really cause significant impact without the attention they need. Classifying vendors means considering factors such as the type of data they access, whether they have direct connectivity to internal systems, whether their disruption would affect critical business processes, and whether they're easily replaceable or represent a single point of dependency. With this classification, it's possible to assign proportional levels of scrutiny: thorough, frequent assessments for critical vendors and simplified processes for low-risk ones. A common mistake is classifying vendors only by the volume of the business relationship, leaving out of the critical category a small vendor that nonetheless has privileged access to a sensitive system that compromises the whole organization if it fails.

This classification isn't a one-off exercise; it must be applied consistently across the organization and updated when a piece of data's context changes, such as when previously public information comes to be considered sensitive after a regulatory change. The practical value shows day to day: a clear classification scheme makes it possible to automate controls, apply encryption or access restrictions only where appropriate, and prioritize the response to an incident according to which specific data was involved.

A frequent example is companies that discover, after an audit or an incident, that they've been retaining personal data for years with no legal basis or defined retention period.

Establishing data lineage, documenting each transformation from the source to the final report, and continuously validating quality isn't just an analytics practice; it's a security requirement that makes it possible to answer with certainty the most basic question in any incident: exactly which data was compromised.

Los datos de entrenamiento y los pesos d: Training data and a model's weights are assets as valuable as an application's source code, but they usually receive much less protection: complete datasets circulate in unencrypted buckets, shared notebooks or repositories with overly broad permissions. It's an especially dangerous threat because it doesn't attack the model in production but its origin, and its effects only show up after deployment, when it's too late to intervene without retraining from scratch. The most common vectors include public or scraped data sources without controls, insiders with access to the data pipeline, and systems that learn continuously from user interaction. Mitigating it requires validating the provenance of each source, applying statistical anomaly detection before training, and establishing baselines of model behavior to detect suspicious deviations after each update.
Buenas prácticas para desplegar modelos: Best practices for deploying models securely
El paso de un modelo de un entorno de pr: Moving a model from a test environment to production introduces risks rarely considered during development: CI/CD pipelines without integrity controls, loosely signed model artifacts, or automatic updates that overwrite a validated version with a compromised one. Securing deployment means versioning and digitally signing each model, validating its provenance before promoting it, and keeping the ability to roll back immediately if an update introduces anomalous behavior or a vulnerability. It's also critical to separate the training, staging and production environments, and to limit who can deploy changes to the active model. A frequent case is teams that update models via notebooks connected directly to production, without a pipeline or approval, which eliminates any traceability and opens the door to errors or manipulations that are hard to detect after the fact.
Cómo se engaña a un modelo con entradas: How a model is fooled with manipulated inputs
Los ataques adversarios consisten en mod: Adversarial attacks consist of minimally and often imperceptibly modifying an input, such as an image or text, so that the model misclassifies it without a human noticing the difference. These changes are calculated by exploiting how the model weights each feature, and can be applied both at inference time, to evade a one-off detection, and systematically to degrade the system's overall performance. It's an especially critical risk in security systems that depend on automated classifiers, such as malware filtering or fraud detection, where an attacker with knowledge of the model can design variants that go unnoticed by the system but keep their malicious behavior. Defending against it means deliberately training with adversarial examples, using model ensembles that make it harder for an attack to transfer, and not relying on a single classifier for critical security decisions.
Cómo funciona el prompt injection y cómo: How prompt injection works and how to mitigate it
El prompt injection consiste en insertar: Prompt injection consists of inserting malicious instructions into a language model's input so it ignores its original rules and carries out unauthorized actions, such as revealing the system prompt, leaking confidential data or running commands in connected tools. It's especially risky in applications that give the model access to APIs, databases or web browsing, because the attack can arrive indirectly, hidden in a document, email or web page the model processes without the user writing it directly. Unlike a classic SQL injection, there's no fixed pattern to block, which forces a combination of input validation, privilege isolation for the tools the model can invoke, and human review of sensitive actions. Ignoring this risk in an assistant connected to internal systems can translate into data leaks or unwanted actions carried out on the user's behalf.
Cómo se roban modelos y cómo prevenirlo: How models are stolen and how to prevent it
El model stealing es una técnica mediant: Model stealing is a technique in which an attacker makes many queries to an exposed model, for example through a public API, and uses the responses obtained to train a substitute model that replicates its behavior without direct access to its weights or training data. The risk goes beyond the loss of intellectual property, since the stolen model also makes it possible to study its weaknesses offline to design more effective adversarial attacks against the original. It's particularly relevant for organizations that expose proprietary models as a service, where each query represents an opportunity for knowledge leakage. Mitigating it requires limiting the query rate per user, obfuscating the precision of responses where possible, and monitoring usage patterns that suggest systematic extraction, such as query volumes far above a legitimate customer's typical use.

Describe los principios de una IA respon: Describes the principles of responsible and transparent AI.
La IA responsable no es solo una declara: Responsible AI isn't just a statement of good intentions, but a set of operational principles that includes transparency about how and with what data a model was trained, explainability of its decisions to those who receive them, accountability for who is responsible when something fails, and fairness in how different groups of users are treated. Applying these principles in practice means documenting the purpose and limitations of each model through model cards, establishing mechanisms for a person to question or appeal an automated decision, and avoiding the use of AI in contexts where its opacity creates a disproportionate risk. A common example is scoring or prioritization models used in hiring or credit processes, where the lack of explainability not only creates distrust but may constitute regulatory non-compliance in jurisdictions that require justifying automated decisions.
Riesgos de privacidad al usar datos pers: Privacy risks when using personal data in AI
Entrenar o ajustar modelos con datos per: Training or fine-tuning models with personal data introduces privacy risks that go beyond simply storing that information: a model can memorize fragments of training data and reveal them in response to a specific query, an attacker can infer whether a specific person was part of the training set through membership inference attacks, and a model's generated responses can combine data from different individuals in a way that re-identifies someone who was originally anonymized. These risks are especially relevant in sectors such as health or finance, where data protection regulations require justifying the legal basis for processing and guaranteeing rights such as erasure, something technically complex once the information has been incorporated into a model's weights. Applying differential privacy during training and minimizing the personal data used are practices that significantly reduce this exposure.
Sesgos algorítmicos y su impacto en la c: Algorithmic bias and its impact on trust
Un modelo entrenado con datos históricos: A model trained on historical data can reproduce and amplify the biases present in that data, systematically favoring or disadvantaging certain groups without any explicit intention to discriminate. From a security perspective, bias isn't just an ethical problem but an operational risk: a biased fraud detection system can generate disproportionate false positives in certain customer segments, eroding trust in the system and creating unnecessary friction, while bias not detected in time can expose the organization to regulatory penalties or reputational damage. Detecting it requires measuring the model's performance broken down by relevant subgroups, not just overall, and setting fairness thresholds as part of the acceptance criteria before a deployment. Ignoring this dimension makes any AI governance program incomplete, however robust its technical controls.
Cómo evaluar riesgos antes de adoptar IA: How to assess risks before adopting AI
Antes de incorporar una solución de IA,: Before adopting an AI solution, whether developed internally or contracted from an external provider, you need to assess the risk it introduces based on the data it will process, the degree of autonomy it will have and the impact of a possible failure or manipulation. This assessment must go beyond a generic security review and include AI-specific questions, such as the origin and quality of the training data, the explainability of the model's decisions, and whether the provider can demonstrate controls against attacks such as prompt injection or data poisoning. Classifying each solution by risk level, similar to how it's done with critical vendors, makes it possible to prioritize controls and prevent a support chatbot from receiving the same level of scrutiny as a model used for credit or medical decisions, where errors have much greater consequences.

Monitoreo y auditoría de modelos ya en p: Monitoring and auditing models already in production
Un modelo que funcionaba correctamente e: A model that worked correctly in initial validation can degrade over time due to the phenomenon known as drift, where real-world data stops resembling the training data, or it can be subject to gradual manipulation if it learns continuously. Continuous monitoring means logging the model's inputs and outputs, periodically measuring performance and fairness metrics, and setting alerts for anomalous usage patterns, such as an unusual volume of queries aimed at extracting information from the model. Auditing, for its part, reviews the logs, the decisions made and the traceability of each deployed version more deeply and periodically. In practice, many organizations deploy a model and consider it finished, without realizing its behavior changes over time until an incident or a user complaint reveals the problem.
Cómo definir políticas internas de uso d: How to define internal AI use policies
Sin una política clara, el uso de IA den: Without a clear policy, AI use within an organization tends to advance chaotically, with teams adopting tools independently, without risk assessment or control over what information is shared with external services. A secure AI use policy should define which tools are approved, what type of data may or may not be processed in them, who authorizes the adoption of a new model or service, and what minimum security and privacy controls are required before integrating it into a business process. It should also address so-called shadow AI, employees' use of AI tools without the security area's knowledge or approval, which represents one of the most common data leak vectors today. Communicating the policy clearly and pairing it with training is as important as writing it, because a policy nobody knows reduces no risk.
